analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal rules on for-profit colleges and gives student borrowers new ways to fight back.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action after its referral to the House Education and Workforce Committee in 2015, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten federal rules on for-profit colleges, which draw most of their revenue from federal student aid and veterans' benefits. It would require those schools to get at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources, ban them from spending federal aid money on recruiting and advertising, and bar forced-arbitration clauses in student contracts so students can sue. It would also let borrowers raise a school's misconduct as a defense against repaying their loans, and create a federal complaint system, an interagency oversight committee, and a public warning list of problem schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future students at for-profit colleges — including veterans and service members using GI Bill and military tuition benefits — along with taxpayers who fund federal student aid.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the required share of revenue that for-profit schools must draw from non-federal sources, from 10% to 15%, or the school risks losing eligibility for federal student aid.

Prohibits colleges from using revenues derived from federal educational assistance funds — including GI Bill and military tuition benefits — for recruiting and marketing, and requires schools getting 65% or more of revenue from federal aid to report advertising spending with independent audit verification.
Bans predispute arbitration agreements in student enrollment contracts and invalidates existing ones, restoring students' right to take disputes to court rather than private arbitration.
Lets a federal student loan borrower, or the Education Department on behalf of a group of borrowers, assert a school's unlawful acts as an affirmative claim or defense against loan repayment.

Creates a centralized complaint tracking system with a toll-free number and website, a coordination committee spanning nine federal agencies including the VA and Pentagon, and an annual public 'Warning List for Parents and Students' naming problem schools.
Protects school employees who report institutional violations from retaliation, with reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees available through the Education Department's Inspector General.

Authorizes civil penalties against schools for substantial misrepresentation — scaled to the institution's default risk and reaching into the millions for repeat violations — with at least half of collected penalties going into a Student Relief Fund for harmed students, and allows state attorneys general to enforce violations in court.

Requires schools with high default rates to give accepted students at least a two-week cooling-off period before enrollment, and to disclose their cohort default rate and licensing-exam pass rates to prospective students.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their shareholders, whose core business model relies on federal student aid, plus the student loan servicing and education-marketing companies that work with them.

drawbacks.text: The 85-15 revenue rule could cut off federal aid to some schools, forcing closures that leave enrolled students without a credential; students at a school that shuts down often lose time and money even if loans are later discharged.

Civil penalties scaled by default risk — up to $3 million multiplied by the school's default-risk figure for repeat violations — fall on the institution, but compliance and legal costs of the bill's extensive new reporting requirements (marketing audits, clinical-training disclosures) could be passed through to tuition.

A good-faith objection supporters would have to acknowledge: risk-based rules can penalize schools precisely for serving low-income students, potentially reducing access to career education for the people the bill is meant to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the documented weak points of the for-profit sector — heavy reliance on federal aid, aggressive recruiting, arbitration clauses that block lawsuits, and default-rate gaming — and most of its protections flow directly to borrowers and veterans. The costs fall on the industry, though some provisions could also harm enrolled students if schools close abruptly under the revenue rule or penalty regime. On balance the design is weighted toward borrower protection, with the sharpest edge pointed at the for-profit college business model.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee in November 2015 and then took no further action — no markup, no vote — before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the PRO Students Act on April 30, 2015, joined by four original cosponsors: Reps. Susan Davis, Steve Cohen, Jackie Speier, and Earl Blumenauer.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day it was introduced.
On November 16, 2015, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training; the record shows no further action of any kind afterward.
The bill gathered 12 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of its provisions ever received a hearing, mark-up, or floor vote in either chamber.
The bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, with all of its student-protection provisions unenacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges and their investors kept full access to federal student aid and veterans' benefits without the revenue limits, marketing bans, arbitration prohibition, or penalties the bill would have imposed. Student borrowers and service members got none of the protections, and taxpayers continued to bear the cost of loans that defaulted at high rates.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 House supporters were Democrats — the sponsor plus 12 cosponsors with no Republicans — and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: For-profit schools collect the bulk of their revenue from federal student aid, GI Bill benefits, and military tuition assistance. The bill would require at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources, bar federal aid money from paying for recruiting and advertising, ban forced-arbitration clauses, expose schools to multi-million-dollar civil penalties and a public warning list, and let borrowers raise school misconduct against their loans — all of which strike at the core revenue and enrollment model of the sector.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: The bill bars predispute arbitration clauses in federal loan servicing contracts, so borrowers could not be forced to give up their day in court, and directs improved servicing and debt collection practices for student loans.

The bill's definition of recruiting and marketing covers third parties paid to supply prospective-student contact information or run enrollment--driving websites, and colleges could no longer pay for it with federal aid revenue — cutting into the lead-generation business that feeds for-profit enrollment.
